label: OLD:repair
name: Fuel on empty coal-barge legs
mech: Anchor: one Kolyma flow rides on the other flow's empty leg. The data reverse the direction. Only about 3 kt of dry cargo goes upstream against 165 kt of coal coming down, so at most 1.8% of the coal could ride on returning barges. The ~165 coal-barge legs going back upstream empty are the real spare capacity. About 17 kt/yr of Northern Delivery fuel would ride those legs in 42 t collapsible fuel bladders, with the coal hold acting as spill containment. That needs 17 of the 165 legs, about 100 bladders and 24 per shoal-limited 1,000 t leg.
value: About 2,100 rub/t for the river leg against 2,700–12,000 rub/t for a dedicated 38–54-year-old tanker (1.3–5.7x). That is under 10% of the delivered diesel price. The real value is not having to replace the tanker fleet.

label: OLD:repair
name: Pre-staged flood-crest barges
mech: Anchor: a loaded barge waits out the ice drift in a sheltered backwater and leaves on the flood crest. Repair: load it in autumn while it is still afloat at a deep berth, so nothing is loaded through ice. It winters in a backwater at least 2.5 m deep, and it is used on a tributary that is navigable only on the spring flood, where there is just one trip a year anyway. With a modelled 12-day recession, a convoy arriving 5–10 days late loses 35–62% of its load. A barge pre-staged at the river mouth goes in full.
value: About 3,100 rub/t against 4,700–11,300 rub/t on that leg today (1.5–3.6x). On the Kolyma main stem the gain is only about 14%.

label: g1_ledger
name: Parallel mid-scale domestic LNG trains
mech: Build Gydan/Yamal LNG as 3–4 parallel trains of 1.5–2.5 Mtpa each, on the Arctic Cascade process. Each train uses domestic electric or UEC-Kuznetsov drives, Arctic air cooling and gravity-base modules, and each comes online as soon as it is built. The closest earlier attempt is Train 4, which stalled at proving the process at 0.9 Mtpa; Arctic LNG 2 failed because its 6.6 Mtpa trains needed imported turbines. This idea stops short of 6.6 Mtpa, so neither the scale-up nor the import limit applies. Colder heat rejection lowers the compressor work per tonne, by the Carnot relation. The deciding quantity is the uptime of a train at 2 Mtpa against the 1,100 $/t/y benchmark of Yamal LNG Trains 1–3.
value: Cuts delivered LNG cost by about 30% (est.) and brings each train into production about a year sooner.

label: g1_ledger
name: Powered-first staged Baimskaya
mech: Start Baimskaya with a 5–8 Mtpa first phase, at an estimated 20–25 kWh per tonne of ore, or about 30 MW. It would run on the spare capacity of the existing Akademik Lomonosov plant and the Pevek line, and its concentrate would ship from Pevek in the NSR window. The full nuclear-powered project would follow later. The closest earlier attempt is KAZ Minerals' 300 kt/y plan, which slipped while it waited for new power and roads. This idea needs neither in its first phase. The deciding quantity is the spare MW at Chaun–Pevek after Bilibino closes.
value: Brings first concentrate several years earlier and puts less capital at risk before any revenue.

label: g1_ledger
name: Plant-chilled foundations
mech: Run a glycol loop through the pile caps of an LNG plant, cooled by its own refrigeration and kept running in summer. Thermosyphons from Fundamentstroyarkos would still cover the winter. A summer heat flux of about 5 W/m² over 1 km² is about 5 MW of heat, or about 2.5 MW of electricity at a COP of 2. That is under 1% of the plant's drive power. The closest earlier attempts are TAPS and the Qinghai–Tibet thermosyphons, which fade as winters warm. An active loop does not depend on how cold the winter is. The deciding quantity is the summer heat flux, measured in boreholes.
value: Holds pile capacity at the design γt for the life of the plant, whatever the warming.

label: g1_neg
name: Numbered-up mid-scale LNG trains
mech: Replicate the Arctic Cascade train built at 0.9 Mtpa about seven times instead of scaling up to 6.6 Mtpa. Each train is driven by 16–25 MW gas turbines already in serial production for Russian pipelines, and Arctic air does the precooling. The closest earlier attempt, Arctic LNG 2, stalled on scarce large turbines; this design avoids that by using drives already built in volume. The deciding quantity is installed capex per tonne-year together with train availability at −45 °C.
value: It phases LNG capital and starts revenue sooner using only domestic drives.

label: g1_neg
name: Underground X-ray ore pre-concentration
mech: Domestic X-ray transmission sorters at the shaft bottom reject waste lumps from disseminated Ni-Cu ore, and the rejected rock becomes stope backfill. The concentrator's fixed capacity then processes more metal per hour. The closest earlier practice, Alrosa's diamond sorting, has never been applied to sulphide ore here. The deciding quantity is the waste-rejection fraction achieved while losing less than 3% of the metal.
value: It raises metal output per unit of existing concentrator capital.

label: g1_neg
name: Re-levelling thaw-tolerant foundations
mech: Surface structures sit on spread footings or space frames with 300 mm hydraulic jacks and are re-levelled from survey data as the active layer moves. The ground is allowed to thaw instead of being kept frozen. The closest earlier attempts, fixed piles and thermosyphons, failed as winters warmed; this design carries no assumed ground-temperature margin. The deciding quantity is the differential settlement rate compared with jack stroke and re-levelling interval.
value: It decouples infrastructure life from the rate of permafrost warming.

label: g1_mech
name: Replicated cold-ambient domestic trains
mech: Copy Train 4 at Yamal and Gydan, which uses a three-stage cascade with cold Arctic air as the heat sink, in place of the APCI/Baker Hughes design, and drive the compressors with domestic electric motors from site power. The closest earlier attempt is Train 4 itself, which ran only at 0.9 Mtpa and needed its piping replaced (F172–174). This plan does not scale the train up; it copies the proven size with corrected alloy piping. The gain is capital: about $73/t, or $1.4/mmBtu, from 1.23x cheaper delivery (est.), assuming the Train 4 capex claim holds. The deciding quantity is train availability, which must be at least 90% across 4 or more trains; test it with two copies built within 4 years.
value: LNG capacity added without Western drives, at about 1.2x lower delivered cost against Yamal T1–3.

label: g1_mech
name: Rock-socketed piles with slip sleeves
mech: Carry new and rebuilt plant loads on bored steel piles set into rock below the frozen ground, and coat the shaft inside the frozen layer with a bitumen slip layer, so thaw adds only small drag load instead of removing the pile's support. Use TMK pipe and Chinese piling rigs. The closest earlier attempts are pile design to SP 25.13330, which has lost 20–55% of capacity (F89), and the Ambarnaya piles set in ice-rich ground (F325). Ground cooling is not involved, so a warming climate does not erode the support. The design applies at Norilsk, Udokan and Baimskaya, but not on deep Yamal sediments. The deciding quantity is depth to competent rock, which must be 30 m or less; test it with load-cell piles monitored for 3–5 thaw seasons.
value: Structure life of 50+ years, for about 1–3% more capex.

label: g1_mech
name: Crusher-conveyor underground ore haulage
mech: Crush ore underground at the level and carry it by fixed belt to the shaft, using Russian-made belts and Ruselprom drives, in place of long truck hauls. A belt uses an estimated 3–5 times less energy per tonne-km and needs far fewer crew and imported spares. The closest earlier attempt is the BelAZ underground truck, still at prototype stage (F184–186); this plan removes most of that fleet instead of replacing it. The deciding quantity is belt availability against a maximum lump size; pilot it on one Talnakh level within 3 years.
value: Full cost at Norilsk down 3–6%, with less reliance on spares for the Western fleet.

label: g1_rf1
name: Numbers-up Arctic Cascade trains
mech: Train 4's 0.9 Mtpa Arctic Cascade design, which is domestic and already running, is copied in series at Utrenneye and Sabetta. Each copy shares the existing gravity base, port, gas gathering and Arc7 berths, instead of scaling to 6.6 Mtpa trains on imported turbines. The closest earlier attempt is Arctic LNG 2, which stalled because only 4 of its 20 Baker Hughes turbines were delivered and the GTE-170 exists only at unit scale. Small trains avoid both by using domestic drives. The deciding quantity is whether series-built trains hold unit capex below $600/t/y once the alloy piping is replaced. Risks are low-temperature metallurgy and efficiency losses at small scale. The test, over 3–5 years, is to build 3 trains, then measure their capex and how many days a year they run.
value: Annualised capital falls about 60% and delivered cost falls about 20–30%, against the Yamal LNG Trains 1–3 benchmark. First LNG comes about 2–3 years after the decision, against 4 for Yamal LNG, with no imported drives.

label: g1_rf1
name: Murmansk winter shuttle loop
mech: In winter, Arc7 ships run only Sabetta/Utrenneye–Murmansk and back, unloading into existing floating storage there. Conventional tankers then carry the LNG onward. The closest earlier attempt is the Zeebrugge transshipment, whose roughly 5,000 km leg wastes scarce Arc7 tonnage and which the EU ban from 2027 closes. The deciding quantity is Arc7 round-trip days in the January–April ice. Risk: storage capacity at Murmansk. The test, over 3 years, is to log turnaround times for the existing ships.
value: The cargo each Arc7 ship delivers per year rises about 1.5–2x (est.), which removes the shipping bottleneck that left Arctic LNG 2 Train 1 unsold. Outbound logistics, the second-largest cost share, falls roughly 25–35%.

label: g1_rf1
name: Grid-first phased Baimskaya
mech: Baimskaya starts at about 15 Mt/y, using its high-grade starter pit. It draws about 60–70 MW from the existing Chaun–Bilibino node and the Akademik Lomonosov plant. A concentrate stockpile holds about 9 months of output and ships in the 3–4 month Pevek window. The RITM-200S units and full 70 Mt/y scale come later, out of cash flow. The closest earlier attempt is the KAZ plan to build all power and infrastructure up front, which pushed capex to about $8bn and moved first production from 2021 to 2027 or later. The benchmark is Red Dog's single 122-day shipping season with a stockpile. The deciding quantity is the firm MW the node can supply. Risks are diseconomies at small scale and tailings in permafrost. The test is to run phase 1 within 4–6 years.
value: Initial capex falls about 60% (est.) and first copper comes 2–3 years earlier, which raises the project's NPV on capital that would otherwise sit idle for years.

label: g1_rf2
name: XRT pre-sorting before milling
mech: X-ray transmission sorters from Rados (Russia) reject low-grade rock ahead of the Natalka and Olimpiada mills, so the mill and reagents treat only feed with gold in it. One quantity decides it: the share of ore mass rejected compared with the share of gold lost in that reject. If 25% of the mass is rejected and ≤5% of the gold goes with it (est., from tests on core), processing cost per ounce falls about 20%. Processing is 30% of TCC, so TCC falls about 6% (est.) and spare mill capacity can take higher-grade feed. The closest earlier attempt is Natalka's planned 2025 flotation retrofit (F66), which raises recovery but still grinds all the waste. Sorting attacks the ground tonnes directly and is domestic and modular. Benchmark: Polyus group recovery of 81.8% (F67). Not suited to Norilsk disseminated ore or Elga coal. Main risk: free gold too fine for X-ray density contrast. Test: core tests in year 1, a 200 t/h module by years 3–4.
value: Gold operations get about 5–8% lower total cash cost per ounce delivered, from domestic equipment, within 4 years.

label: g1_rf2
name: Cold-calendar maintenance shift
mech: Planned overhauls and major component changes at the Natalka, Udokan and Elga pits move into January–February at −40 to −50 °C. Fleet failure rates rise up to 6–7x in that period (F111). In the warmer months the whole fleet runs. Arctic-grade oils from Gazpromneft and Lukoil and Teplostar preheaters keep the trucks that do run in the cold working. One quantity decides it: the share of overhaul hours that can be moved compared with the hours lost to cold failures. If the 8% of fleet hours spent on planned overhaul land on cold days (est.), effective tonnes per year rise 3–6% (est.). Fixed cost is spread over more tonnes, so unit cost falls 2–4%. The closest earlier attempts, the Zyfra and BelAZ autonomous haulage pilots (F196), add technology but do not change when failures happen. Benchmarks: Kupol and Diavik. Main risks: workshop space and spares lead times (F63). Test: a 2-year A/B trial on two fleets at one site.
value: The same open-pit fleets gain more days of operation per year, with almost no capital.

label: g1_rf2
name: Triaged thermosyphon pile retrofit
mech: Borehole temperatures plus InSAR rank plant foundations by remaining pile capacity. Retrofit GET/VET thermosyphons from Fundamentproekt then go only on the Norilsk and Talnakh structures headed toward a loss of more than 40% (F89). One quantity decides it: the air freezing index compared with the heat flowing into the pile. Norilsk's long, deep winter still gives a strong cooling margin. TAPS and Qinghai–Tibet lost cooling where winters were weak (F320–322), so the scheme is limited to the coldest sites and leaves out Salekhard and Nadym. The closest earlier attempt, post-spill monitoring (F18), detected thaw but fixed nothing. Benchmark: Ambarnaya and the 35% deformed-building share (F252). Main risk: non-condensable gas fade, so inspect every 3 years. Test: an instrumented pilot on 20 piles with 3 seasons of monitoring.
value: Avoids unplanned plant outages and prolongs infrastructure life on thawing ground, at a small share of Norilsk's ~$3bn/yr capex.

label: repair
name: Hull-paced domestic Arctic Cascade trains
mech: The anchor is unchanged: copy the domestic 0.9 Mtpa Arctic Cascade Train 4 many times instead of building 6.6 Mtpa trains that need imported or first-of-kind drives. In the repaired design, trains are added only at Sabetta and only as fast as Arc7 hulls arrive. Each train needs about 0.55 hull: a hull carries about 1.63 Mt/y when it runs 150 days a year east on the NSR and spends the winter shuttling 12-day round trips to the Saam/Ura FSU near Murmansk. In winter this shuttle replaces the 20-day Zeebrugge run, which the EU bans from 2027. With this matching, all added output can be shipped year-round, which fixes the kill metric. The trains have two roles. First, they are a domestic-drive hedge for the Nuovo Pignone strings on Trains 1–3: each 1% of availability lost there is 0.165 Mt/y. Second, they are the growth path once Arctic LNG 2's idle 13.2 Mtpa is full. That needs about 8 hulls, so it happens around 2030–33 at 1–2 hulls a year from Zvezda. No new trains go to Utrenneye before then.
value: Full delivered cost is about $236/t, against $295/t for a Yamal T1–3-type train (1.25x) and $257/t for a large domestic-drive train (1.09x). First LNG is about 3 years after the decision for a series copy, against 4–4.5. But it is 1.5x worse than simply filling Arctic LNG 2's idle trains, which is why it is held back until those are full.

label: repair
name: Level-crusher conveyor decline for Talnakh
mech: The anchor is unchanged: crush ore at the level and carry it on a fixed belt, replacing truck haulage. The belt no longer stops at an existing shaft. It runs up a 14° decline all the way to surface, and serves as the hoisting route for the Talnakh concentrator expansion from 10 to 18 Mtpa in place of a new 2.1 km skip shaft. Nornickel's shafts advanced only 150–322 m in 2017, so sinking takes 6.5–14 years, plus about 1.5 years to equip. A 4.1 km decline (1,000 m lift) driven by drill-and-blast from 2–3 headings at 150 m/month takes about 1–2.3 years, plus about 1 year to install the belt. It is lifted by three flights of ST3150 belt (or two of ST5000) at 1,600 t/h, drawing 5.1 MW, or 3.2 kWh/t against 3.4 for a skip.
value: Cost per tonne of ore is $2.9–4.0, against $3.6–5.3 for a new shaft. That is only about 1–2% of full cost per tonne of nickel-equivalent, so the gain is not cost. The gain is ore 4–11 years sooner for 8 Mt/y, worth about $1.5–3.5bn PV. That holds only if hoisting is what limits the expansion.

label: repair
name: Cold-margin triaged thermosyphon retrofit
mech: Anchor: borehole temperatures plus InSAR rank existing foundations by remaining pile capacity, and retrofit thermosyphons only on the worst ones, only where the winter is cold enough. The cutoff is now a computed number: the cooling margin M, which is winter heat a unit can pull out of the ground divided by the yearly heat flowing in per pile. In 2050 climate (+2.5 K in winter), M is 1.53 at Norilsk, 2.10 at Udachny/Mirny and 1.57 at Pevek, which pass the M ≥ 1.5 cutoff. It is 1.05 at Salekhard, 0.88 at Nadym, 0.90 at Fairbanks and 0.41 at Beiluhe on the Qinghai–Tibet line, which fail. That ranking matches where cooling was actually seen to fade on the Trans-Alaska pipeline (TAPS) and the Qinghai–Tibet line (F320–321). Triage step 0 is the cheapest fix: reopen crawlspace vents and repair utility leaks. Only structures that keep warming after that get vertical units drilled with low-headroom rigs from the ventilated crawlspace, or inclined units from the outside edge for buildings under about 20 m wide. That is about 50 of the 165 monitored Norilsk/Talnakh structures and about 8,500 units. Each unit finishes cooling the ground to the target in about one winter.
value: It keeps structures on thawing ground in service past 2050 for about $64M, against $198M for retrofitting all 165 structures and $196–392M for new piles to bedrock. That is about 3× cheaper than either. It adds only about $3–19 per t Ni-eq (0.04–0.20% of full cost) and avoids an expected $26–86M/yr of thaw-related losses.

label: repair
name: Shaft-bottom XRT sorting, hoist-bound mines
mech: Anchor: domestic X-ray transmission (XRT) sorters at the shaft bottom reject waste lumps before hoisting, and the rejects go straight into stope backfill. The repair moves it from "freeing concentrator capacity" to deep mines where the 2.1 km shafts set the limit, such as Skalisty and the Talnakh/Oktyabrskoye deep levels. There every tonne of waste rejected below ground is replaced by ore in the fixed skip capacity. With the fines (about 35% of ore) bypassing the sorter, metal hoisted per year rises ×1.095 at Selebi-type results (15% rejected, 2% metal lost) and ×1.36 at stringer-type results (44%, 4%). After counting the metal lost for good in the backfill, metal NPV is still ×1.085–1.31 over a 30-year reserve at 14%. Two or three 150 t/h units cover 2 Mt/yr hoisted. Rejects of at most 0.41 t per t of ore fit in the backfill needed (0.44–0.67 t per t), so no tailings go to the surface. The design is restricted to cuprous/stringer and massive ores at contacts. Disseminated Norilsk-1 and Maslovskoye ore is left out (16% metal loss at 23% rejection on disseminated test ore), as are mines where hoisting is not the limit.
value: Each extra tonne of Ni-eq from a hoist-bound deep mine costs $5.0–8.3k by sorting against $6.7–12.6k from a new deep shaft, 1.2–1.8× cheaper. It comes in about 2–3 years instead of about 10 years of shaft sinking.
